summary: The Vakatakas rose in the Vidarbha region of the northern Deccan around 250 under Vindhyashakti, and his son Pravarasena I, the only Vakataka to call himself samrat (emperor), spread their rule widely. After him the family split into a main line at Nandivardhana and Pravarapura and a cadet line at Vatsagulma; a marriage to the Guptas around 380–390 drew the main line into the Gupta orbit. Harishena of Vatsagulma, patron of the Ajanta caves, was the last great king, and Vakataka rule faded out in the early 6th century.
details: In the 3rd century the Deccan was divided among regional kingdoms. One of them was founded around 250 by Vindhyashakti, a chief named after Vindhyavasini, a goddess of the Vindhya hills. Very little is known about him: later records call him the 'banner of the Vakataka family', and Puranic tradition links him to Vidisha. He ruled until about 275. His family came to control Vidarbha, in what is now eastern Maharashtra, and would become the leading power of the northern Deccan for more than two centuries.

Vindhyashakti's son Pravarasena I ruled for some sixty years, from about 275 to 335. He was the only Vakataka king to take the imperial title samrat, and he performed many grand Vedic sacrifices that advertised his power. His rule is said to have stretched across much of central India and the northern Deccan, making the Vakatakas one of the strongest dynasties of their time. His eldest son Gautamiputra died before him, so the succession passed to a grandson, and the family's unity did not outlast him.

On Pravarasena I's death around 335 the kingdom was divided among his descendants. Two branches are known. The main line, under his grandson Rudrasena I, ruled from Nandivardhana (Nagardhan, near Nagpur) in eastern Vidarbha. A younger son, Sarvasena, founded a separate line with its capital at Vatsagulma (Washim) in the west, and is credited with a lost Prakrit poem, the Harivijaya. The two branches lived side by side for about 150 years, each with its own kings, until Harishena of Vatsagulma reunited them late in the 5th century.

To the north, the Gupta king Samudragupta was building an empire across the Ganges plain. His inscription on the Allahabad pillar lists the kings he overthrew, among them a 'Rudradeva'. Some historians identify him with the Vakataka king Rudrasena I, who ruled from Nandivardhana from about 335 to 360; others reject the link, and the question is unsettled. Either way, the Gupta empire now bordered the Vakataka lands, and relations with the Guptas would shape the main Vakataka branch for the next century.

Rather than fight the Guptas, the Vakatakas made an alliance with them. Rudrasena II, king of the main branch from about 385, married Prabhavatigupta, a daughter of the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II and his queen Kuberanaga. The match gave Chandragupta a friendly ally on the southern flank of his empire and tied the two royal houses closely together. Rudrasena II died after a reign of only about five years, leaving three young sons and a widow whose family ruled northern India.

When Rudrasena II died around 390, none of his sons was an adult, so Prabhavatigupta governed as regent in the name of the eldest, Divakarasena. She ruled for about twenty years; one of her land grants, found at Pune, is dated in her thirteenth year. She seems to have kept power even after her son came of age. Gupta influence over the Vakatakas peaked in these years, and some historians describe the kingdom as practically part of the Gupta empire, though the evidence for direct Gupta control is thin.

Prabhavatigupta's son Pravarasena II ruled the main branch from about 420 to 455. He is the best-documented Vakataka king, known from seventeen copper-plate land grants. He moved the capital from Nandivardhana to a new city, Pravarapura, at Paunar near Wardha, where he built a temple to Rama. He is also credited with the Setubandha, a celebrated poem in Maharashtri Prakrit about Rama's bridge to Lanka. His long and settled reign marked the cultural high point of the eastern Vakataka kingdom.

Pravarasena II was followed by his son Narendrasena, who ruled from about 455 (some accounts say 440) to 480. The close Gupta tie of his grandmother's time had loosened, and the Vakatakas acted as a power in their own right. Vakataka influence spread northward into central India. But the main branch was soon under pressure: Narendrasena's son Prithivishena II, the last known king of this line, was defeated by the Vishnukundina king Madhava Varma II from the eastern Deccan.

Harishena of the Vatsagulma branch was the last great Vakataka king. He probably annexed the weakened main branch, and an inscription in Ajanta Cave XVI credits him with conquests from Gujarat and Malwa to Kalinga and Andhra. He and his courtiers, such as the minister Varahadeva and the vassal Upendragupta, sponsored the magnificent Buddhist caves and paintings at Ajanta. His dates are disputed: the dynasty's genealogy places him c. 475–510, while the art historian Walter Spink dates his reign 460–477 and most of the Ajanta work to c. 460–480.

Harishena was followed by two kings whose names are not known, and the end of the dynasty is obscure. One view holds that the Kalachuris of Mahishmati overthrew them. A later Sanskrit tale, the Dashakumaracharita, describes a pleasure-loving last king killed fighting an invasion led by the Kadambas near the Wardha river. A Kadamba record of 519 suggests the Kadambas had annexed the region after about 500. By then the Vakataka kingdom had disappeared, and within a few decades the Chalukyas of Badami would rise as the new power of the Deccan.
